name: Katie Kaminski
one_paragraph: Katie (Katy) Kaminski, a trend-following researcher (AlphaSimplex) and Systematic Investor co-host, sees markets as a sequence of macro themes (inflation, policy divergence, geopolitics, AI growth, deglobalisation) that trend followers capture by following price rather than forecasting, so she makes money by staying unbiased, liquid and adaptable, diversified across speeds, parameters, markets and managers. Her central research claims are that higher inflation turns the stock-bond correlation positive and breaks the bond leg of 60/40, so long/short trend in bonds, dollar, gold and commodities is the repair; that geopolitical (supply-side) risk leads inflation and pays trend through commodities and bonds; that trend is a second responder that loses early in short, reversing shocks and drawdowns under about 15% and pays in deeper, longer dislocations; and that return dispersion among trend managers is a fingerprint of design choices (speed, market set, vol sizing, carry share) that rotate year to year, so no one choice can be picked in advance. She advises holding trend as a reactive core (about 15-20% in a 60/40), rebalancing into drawdowns rather than timing, giving each holding a role, judging strategies out of sample with robust parameters, and treating trend plus equities as a jointly risk-managed pair because alpha and beta are not fully separable. Her evidence is her own and peers' papers, factor regressions and long histories, with open admission of short samples; her recurring caution is that bonds, fixed-income trend and fast-reversing shocks are where trend is weakest.

core_beliefs.belief: Trend following is a rules-based, direction-agnostic response to whichever macro theme prevails; it needs no forecast of which theme or when. It thrives on macro change, disruption and boom-bust cycles (2022, 2026, 'we like chaos') and does poorly in steady markets, in consolidation before a new theme, and in sudden shocks that reverse.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - same framing from Aug 2024 to Oct 2026; the 'chaos is good' and 'shocks are bad' statements are reconciled only by shock type (see internal_tensions)

core_beliefs.belief: Return dispersion among trend managers is structural and larger than people expect. It comes from design choices (signal speed, market set / risk allocated to the few big trends, vol-sizing speed, share of non-trend signals such as carry). No single choice wins every year, no style factor persists, and the best choice cannot be known ex ante; large moves amplify small design differences.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - one qualification: in Dec 2024 she could not say statistically that 2024 dispersion was above normal (MT195-C03-5), while in MT002 she called it large

core_beliefs.belief: Diversify rather than pick: across lookbacks and methods, parameter schools (fixed/dynamic, recent/long data, per-market/common), markets (include everything, let the signal decide) and two or three different managers. Any single choice banks on one view of the world.
core_beliefs.stable: stable - she does favour a large-market tilt in a small universe only as 'a different strategy' (MT195-C05-X1)

core_beliefs.belief: Speed: longer lookbacks have a slightly higher Sharpe and win in calm/slow years (2024), but shorter, more reactive signals give convexity, pivot points and crisis alpha (Covid). The best speed depends on the year's path and on the client objective (Sharpe vs equity-conditional protection). The mid-range (4-9 months; 6-8 months) is the worst place in a V-shaped shock year (2025); the industry has drifted slower over time.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - Aug 2024 she leaned toward considering shorter signals in a divergent world (MT021-C04-3), then 2024 results favoured slow (MT195, MT120), then 2025 favoured both ends; her conclusion is always 'no speed always wins'

core_beliefs.belief: Inflation makes bonds behave badly: with higher inflation the stock-bond correlation turns positive and bond volatility rises (about 4% to about 6%), so bonds lose their safe-haven role and a static 60/40 loses its safety leg. Long/short trend in bonds (and dollar, gold, commodities) repairs this because it can be short when bonds fall.
core_beliefs.stable: stable with nuance - Oct 2024: with inflation at 2-2.5% the classic risk-off pattern returned (MT086-C09-1); Oct 2026: bonds are fine when yield compensates (MT191-C07-3); throughout she says inflation comes in waves

core_beliefs.belief: Crisis alpha is something trend searches for, not a guaranteed hedge. It needs a strategy that is unbiased, liquid and adaptable, and a sustained dislocation (weeks to months); fast-reversing shocks (Aug 2024 yen unwind, Liberation Day) give none. Trend loses in the first phase of equity drawdowns under about 15% and pays in deeper/longer ones (second responder).
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - wording only: 'crisis alpha' becomes 'second responder' (2025-26) because insurance-style narratives did not help investors hold it (MT191-C10-X2 / MT191-C11-X1)

core_beliefs.belief: Geopolitical risk, especially supply-side, leads inflation (2-3 years of higher inflation, lower growth). Trend profits in the biggest geopolitical-risk months through commodities and bonds (the inflation channel), not equities; a risk premium for it is being repriced now.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - Jan 2026 a preview of unpublished research; Apr 2026 a paper in progress; Jun 2026 results (monthly sample since 2000); Oct 2026 the central thesis. Direction of the claim unchanged

core_beliefs.belief: Do not time trend. Returns come from a few big months (without the 20 largest months the average falls from 5.6% to about -0.5%), investors lose much of it by timing, and trend mean-reverts at strategy level (great years followed by weak ones and vice versa). Hold it with a defined role, rebalance into it after drawdowns and trim after gains.

Trend drawdowns happen in calm, equity-friendly, low-vol conditions and recover faster when equities are stressed; trend therefore looks good coming out of a drawdown in either state. Its convexity shows in the worst equity quintiles, where price changes matter more than fundamentals.

Price trend and economic (macro) trend are complements (40-50% correlated): economic trend filters headline noise and wins when fundamentals are clear and calm; price trend wins in stress and when fundamentals are irrelevant. Macro managers and trend followers harvest mostly the same global trends by different entry methods; economic trend is 'more art'.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - which one wins flips with the year (macro better in 2025 headline chaos, price better in early 2026), not the belief itself

core_beliefs.belief: Trend plus equities is a natural complement, but 'portable alpha' is not truly separable: trend can be long equities, so alpha and beta can draw down together. Futures give capital-efficient exposure; combine and risk-manage the two jointly and rebalance rather than stack naively. A total-portfolio view values trend more than a bucket view.

Research standard: judge strategies out-of-sample and by stability when parameters are permuted; prefer walk-forward tests and non-parametric filters to rule-based regime definitions; estimation error is large so use only what can be estimated (volatility, a little correlation) and aim to be approximately right. Judge replication by tracking error, not returns.

Volatility estimation is calibration, not alpha. Static vs dynamic sizing is a spectrum (static: more concentration in big winners and residual long-vol; dynamic: cuts risk at reversals). Fast vs slow vol adjustment helps or hurts depending on the path (2022 bond vol doubling, Liberation Day, H1 vs H2 2025). Volatility gives the range, not the direction.

Fixed income is the hardest sector for trend (many dimensions move at once; monetary-policy expectations ebb and flow; the market prices cuts before they come, so only a surprise relative to pricing starts a trend). Rates/FX are whipsawed in policy-uncertain regimes. Central banks no longer moving in sync create tactical opportunity.

Carry and other convergent strategies inside CTA portfolios smooth returns in calm times but dilute crisis alpha and lose in violent short events (Covid, Aug 2024); relative-value carry with leverage is most dangerous, unlevered directional carry less so. Inside trend books the share of non-trend signals is a source of dispersion.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - in March 2026 she notes FX and energy carry worked while bond carry did not (MT083-C05-4)

core_beliefs.belief: Crowding concerns about CTAs are overstated because they trade very liquid markets with small AUM. Crowding can be proxied by excess co-movement (reversal risk, but crowded trades can extend through feedback); capacity-limited markets may have looked better in backtests when fewer people traded them.
core_beliefs.stable: evolved - Dec 2024 crowding was rewarded and a crowding cut would have hurt (MT002-C06-2); 2026 not a concern in liquid markets; 2025 capacity-limited markets flagged as a possible backtest illusion

core_beliefs.belief: Replication gives CTA beta-like exposure, not the index: index replication (regression) is slow, mechanical replication has one parameter set and dispersion; a blend lowers tracking error but it stays high. Replicators beat many CTAs in 2025 because they are smaller in market set and slower, not by luck.

Sentiment and behaviour matter for trend: the follower is behaviour-focused, markets in transition swing between fear and optimism, familiar assets feel safer than they are, and investors chase returns; institutions detach emotion through process and change allocations after governance shocks.

mechanisms.name: Inflation turns bonds from hedge to risk asset
chain: higher inflation regime -> stock-bond correlation positive and bond vol up (about 4% to about 6%)
bonds fall with equities and are marked to market -> locked-in yield does not protect (2022)
inflation arrives in waves / geopolitical supply shock -> bond vol stays high even as CPI falls
static 60/40 loses its safety leg -> long/short trend in bonds (can be short) restores negative correlation
mechanisms.fails_when: Inflation is low (classic flight-to-safety, right-shifted bond returns) or yields are high enough to compensate; samples from 1990 hold few high-rate periods

mechanisms.name: Geopolitical risk to inflation to trend payoff
chain: supply-side geopolitical-risk spike -> structural inflation risk premium and commodity/energy shock
inflation shock expectation -> bonds fall, dollar and energy rise; equities depend on whether growth is hit
adaptive multi-asset trend -> gains in commodities and fixed income in the largest GPR-rise months (and falls), 'smile'
bonds fail as hedge -> 60/40 vulnerable; commodities respond first, trend second
mechanisms.fails_when: Monthly data cannot show slow-building events (tech bubble); a risk-off move can reverse equity-long/bond-short positioning; dollar and energy patterns could differ over longer samples

mechanisms.name: Shock type and equity-drawdown depth decide the trend payoff
chain: shock runs against prevailing positions (long equities) -> trend loses in the first phase (drawdown under about 15%)
exogenous shock that reverses within days (Liberation Day, Aug 2024) -> whipsaw, too short to detect
drawdown deepens/lengthens (tech bubble, GFC, 2022) or shock is endogenous (monetary policy, inflation, valuation shift) -> trend repositions and pays as second responder
magnitude-of-surprise (multi-day) is bad for CTAs; correlation surprises mark inflection points that drive dispersion
mechanisms.fails_when: Few data points above 15% drawdown; one-off events lack significance; Liberation Day is outside her turbulence data; an exogenous shock that extends can help

mechanisms.name: Speed, market set and vol sizing become manager dispersion
chain: profits come from a few big trends -> risk allocated to those trends sets relative performance (gold only vs wider metals)
a V-shaped / noisy year -> short and very long windows survive, mid-range (4-9m, 6-8m) overreacts
faster vol estimation cuts risk sooner -> good if the shock reverses, bad if the trend continues
different designs -> different return paths; best choice flips from year to year
mechanisms.fails_when: Path dependent; best speed or set cannot be chosen ex ante; narrow market sets look smart only while their assets trend

mechanisms.name: Why investors earn less than trend (behavioural cost)
chain: trend returns are punchy -> a few months drive the return (20 largest months)
investors sell after underperformance and buy after strong runs -> dollar-weighted return far below index
liquid daily-dealing vehicles and short-term attention amplify timing; patience is asymmetric across asset classes
remedy: defined roles, expectations, long-term benchmarks, rebalancing, packaged/model-portfolio products
mechanisms.fails_when: Anonymous daily-liquid ETF holders cannot be coached; governance shocks force re-evaluation

mechanisms.name: Price trend vs economic trend
chain: headline risk -> price trends noisy
economic trend follows overall themes -> filters noise while fundamentals stay positive (2025, S&P +16%)
in stress fundamentals become irrelevant -> price trend dominates and shows convexity in worst equity quintiles
mechanisms.fails_when: Macro indicators can predict a trend that never occurs; economic trend is 'more art'; official data can go missing (40-day US gap)

mechanisms.name: Carry dilutes crisis alpha
chain: pure trend struggles for years -> managers add carry/convergent sleeves for smoother returns
violent short event (Covid, Aug 2024 yen unwind) -> carry sleeves lose, pure/faster trend copes better
large carry allocation -> less ability to capture crisis alpha
mechanisms.fails_when: Carry sleeve is small or unlevered directional

mechanisms.name: Trend drawdown timing relative to equities
chain: equities at new highs, benign conditions -> trend drawdowns and slower recovery
equity stress -> faster recovery
trend mean-reverts at long horizons -> rebalance into it, do not time it
blending trend with the S&P gives nearly the sum of returns (host's illustration)
mechanisms.fails_when: Start of the next recovery is unknown; next recovery could be slow or fast

mechanisms.name: Replication blend lowers tracking error
chain: index replication infers industry positions by regression -> aggregate view but slow, backward-looking, chunky
mechanical replication is a real simplified strategy -> reacts to markets but one parameter set and dispersion
informed regression combines both -> lower tracking error, still high
mechanisms.fails_when: Both break down in different environments; neither delivers the index

mechanisms.name: Alternative-market trend lagged on sector regime
chain: 2020-22 shocks (Covid, Ukraine) -> gas and power, credit trended extremely (40-50% of outperformance from gas and power)
those assets range-bound -> alternative-market managers lagged about three years
alternative markets are a diversification argument (low-correlation P&L streams raise Sharpe) net of higher costs
mechanisms.fails_when: Exotic contract costs reduce net Sharpe; only about 10 years of history; crowding untested

mechanisms.name: Fixed income trend depends on regime and surprise
chain: falling rates with steep curve -> strong long; inverted curve -> strong short; flat -> mixed
market already prices Fed cuts (SOFR vs fed funds) -> signals stay weak and mixed
only an outcome different from pricing (far more cuts, or no cut) -> large move and trend catalyst
mechanisms.fails_when: If futures price future rather than current rates (host), long yields can rise after cuts

mechanisms.name: Excess co-movement as crowding gauge
chain: common theme (e.g. tariffs) moves precious metals together beyond asset-class beta -> excess co-movement
excess co-movement -> higher reversal risk, or an extended trend through feedback trading
mechanisms.fails_when: Direction ambiguous, so used as filter/risk tool/attribution, not a stand-alone signal

mechanisms.name: Static vs dynamic volatility sizing
chain: trending market -> volatility expands in the direction of the trend
static sizing -> concentration in big winners and residual long-vol (about 20% correlation to long vol)
vol also spikes at reversals (cocoa 20% to 120%) -> dynamic sizing cuts risk at turning points
hence higher Sharpe with scaling, higher return without (Quantica 1994-2024)
mechanisms.fails_when: Different 30-year period with other outlier frequency; effect partly endogenous

playbook.rule: Core trend signal: classic 12-month momentum long/short; diversify lookbacks and methods, aggregate several trend measures, adjust for changing volatility, avoid single-parameter implementations (100-day vs 105-day example). Treat speed as a benchmark of market frequency; consider smoothing, trade frequency, nonlinear/ML time-varying speed.
playbook.why: Best window is idiosyncratic by year; simple parameters create dispersion; 12-month has the higher Sharpe

playbook.rule: Keep some reactivity; tilt speed by asset class only marginally and only to the level of statistical evidence; keep a toolkit of speeds because reactivity helps in fast crises while cost rises with speed.
playbook.why: Slow-only systems cannot pivot; long-premium systems look like equities; evidence for speed specialisation is slim

playbook.rule: Combine price trend with economic trend (40-50% correlated) for the mandate; risk-mitigation clients keep price trend for stress behaviour. Use global, not only US, economic data and watch CPI/PCE as focal points.
playbook.why: Natural complements through regimes; missing US data only partly blinds

playbook.rule: Read breadth of trend signals across asset classes: balanced signals with no standout mean consolidation before the next big trend; a shift of aggregate positioning to long bonds / short commodities signals repricing of recession expectations.
playbook.why: Trend signals show where the market is going without forecasting

playbook.rule: Look for fundamental data confirming a new direction rather than trading rhetoric-driven shocks (e.g. copper tariffs and copper).
playbook.why: Rhetoric shocks are often bad for trend

playbook.rule: Include all markets, including metals, softs and currencies; do not drop markets that backtested poorly; keep secondary metals (silver, platinum, copper) rather than only the ten most liquid; include alternative markets for diversification accounting for costs.
playbook.why: Assets that never trended (metals, cocoa) started trending when macro changed; ten-asset set underperformed a wide basket for 10 years

playbook.rule: Allocate risk, not notional: size every asset by volatility (10% vol FX vs 40% vol commodities = 4:1) and signal strength; expected return = estimated Sharpe (about 0.4-0.5) times vol allocated.
playbook.why: Volatility estimation is calibration; risk is what trend allocates

playbook.rule: Sit between static and dynamic vol sizing depending on vol window, reactivity and objective; positions shrink as vol expands (built-in profit taking).
playbook.why: Risk mitigation vs risk-adjusted return; path dependence

playbook.rule: Put correlations in the risk model (stock-bond correlation sign matters) but stay sceptical of their volatility; decide how much to include shocks/jumps in vol estimates (nickel event); do not use a model with a long-run negative stock-bond correlation.
playbook.why: Correlation says where risk is; assuming negative understates risk when positive

playbook.rule: Do not change the model after a one-off shock such as Liberation Day; re-examine how vol estimation and signals react to sustained shocks. In a drawdown rerun existing analysis on the data instead of reacting; stick to process, do not sell on VIX headlines.
playbook.why: Three days is not statistically significant; sellers at the low missed the rebound

playbook.rule: Do not try to capture one-day extreme moves; short-term trend needs costly execution infrastructure and out-of-sample testing; ETF-wrapped strategies run lower turnover in markets that market makers can hedge.
playbook.why: Catching extreme days means bearing cost on all other days; ETF intraday liquidity

playbook.rule: Rank strategies first on out-of-sample results and stability when about five parameters are permuted, then downside capture, upside capture and Sharpe; use walk-forward tests accounting for variables tried; prefer non-parametric similarity filters to rule-based regimes.
playbook.why: Easy to overfit the past

playbook.rule: Build CTA style factors by perturbing one design decision at a time vs a benchmark trend system and regress manager returns on them; track yearly; study hypothetical managers and random-signal experiments instead of one backtest.
playbook.why: Disentangle benchmark from style tilts; avoid cherry-picking

playbook.rule: Condition on equity drawdowns ignoring equity positions and read long/short positioning in other asset classes in each crisis; use longer histories (to the 1970s) only for single-asset-class signals such as bonds.
playbook.why: See what a defensive pivot implies; long multi-asset backtests need heavy assumptions

playbook.rule: Measure a risk before managing it: use public series (geopolitical risk index by country, threat vs act), sort months by largest increases and decreases because GPR is non-stationary, then look at asset and strategy returns; use turbulence (magnitude-of-surprise / correlation-surprise) metrics for shock size.
playbook.why: If a quant cannot measure it, it cannot be managed

playbook.rule: Judge replication on tracking error and goodness of fit, not returns; evaluate alternative markets by Sharpe per market adjusted for period and portfolio theory, not recent sector winners.
playbook.why: Ex post one can always select the best past return; 10-year history is short

playbook.rule: Hold trend as a reactive core: about 15-20% (Quantica mixes 55/35/10 in low cash-rate regimes vs 55/25/20 in high), added in drawdowns not after gains; add long-short trend in bonds, dollar, gold, commodities to 60/40 instead of long-only bonds or gold.
playbook.why: Timing the next trend is a fool's game; long-only add-ons correlate in equity-down periods

playbook.rule: Layer defensives by role (first responder commodities, second responder trend, third responder others) against inflation and geopolitical threats, not just equity drawdowns; get commodity exposure actively (commodity risk or trend), not via passive energy-heavy indices; buy bonds when yield compensates.
playbook.why: Roles help investors hold through bad periods; commodities lack carry and are volatile

playbook.rule: Keep carry exposure limited and directional with controlled leverage when combined with trend; avoid levered relative-value carry.
playbook.why: Large carry waters down crisis alpha

playbook.rule: Start simple: pick two or three different CTAs (faster crisis-alpha manager plus slower or replication product); do not read a 400-500bp gap vs the index as poor selection; match design to client objective and educate investors on dispersion.
playbook.why: No style factor persists; gaps arise by chance

playbook.rule: Where trend and equities are combined, size trend dynamically, cap equity beta in the trend book or accept independence; use portable alpha only after checking that alpha and beta drawdowns can coincide; package equities plus trend where investors cannot hold trend separately.
playbook.why: Shared equity exposure; holdability

playbook.rule: Pick market mix by objective: liquid traditional markets for crisis alpha and cash efficiency, broader alternatives for long-run Sharpe; remove equity and trend exposure from macro managers' returns to measure alpha.
playbook.why: Different objective functions give different optimal portfolios

playbook.rule: Institutions: set a target, role, expectations and long-term benchmark and rebalance; slow decision frequency; reach private wealth through ETFs and model-portfolio providers.
playbook.why: More frequent decisions produce more adverse emotional decisions

evidence_style: Academic and empirical. Cites her own papers and studies (crisis alpha, Bonds Behaving Badly, Trend Following in a Defensive Rotation, CTA style factors and CTA style evolution, drawdown paper, turbulence metrics, Trade War: Crisis or Correction, replication papers, geopolitical-risk and managed-futures paper) plus peers (Quantica, AQR, Man AHL, Harvey et al., Caldara-Iacoviello GPR). Prefers a data study over a qualitative statement, writes a paper after emotional events to counter emotion, uses charts of drawdown depth/duration, quintile plots, factor regressions, hypothetical-manager simulations and long histories (to 1970s, '800 years' of bond data). Argues from first principles (portfolio theory, estimation error, 1/N) and practitioner experience with clients. Open about sample limits (post-1990, monthly frequency, one-off events, about 10 years of alternative-market data) and about what she has not tested (China CTAs, correlation-conditional trend, replication tracking-error numbers). Rarely gives numbers on her own trading or P&L.

views_timeline.view: Trend signals are moving from a soft-landing profile (short bonds, long equities, long commodities, long dollar) toward a recession-type one (weak, still slightly long equities, long bonds, short commodities, neutral dollar); markets at an inflection with fast sentiment shifts; falling CPI does not make bonds safe; the 5 Aug move was an equity/carry-unwind shock, not classic risk-off; no crisis alpha yet.
views_timeline.reasoning: Visible in trend positioning after the August shock; inflation comes in waves; quick reversal fails the sustained-loss condition

views_timeline.view: Soft-landing consensus is the main risk; renewed inflation with rates paused and higher for longer could drive next year's trends; trend signals balanced across asset classes with no standout, an inflection point before the next big trend; summer defensive positioning resembles early 2020; post-2008 low-rate regime unlikely to return.
views_timeline.reasoning: A trend follower asks what investors are underestimating; consolidation precedes new trends

views_timeline.view: 2024 was won by slow, big-market trend; fast signals were hurt by policy-expectation noise. Trend signals long US equities, short fixed income, long dollar in size after a V-shaped dollar move; dollar trend may continue short term, long run unclear; wider macro outcomes likely.
views_timeline.reasoning: Style-factor spreads; pro-growth outlook and cautious Fed

views_timeline.view: Biggest underestimated 2025 risk is the volatility of inflation (bonds hard for investors and trend); US-vs-world dollar trade has legs but faces policy, geopolitical and trade-conflict risk; optimistic for trend into 2025 because turbulence is what it likes; sentiment extremes are warnings.
views_timeline.reasoning: Bonds have no natural predator except inflation; US deficit and policy uncertainty

views_timeline.view: A year of starts and stops: post-election trade (long US equities, short bonds, long dollar) unwound while markets test whether US exceptionalism has wings; policymakers cannot force yields down if inflation rises; possible BoJ hike makes carry a question; 'we are not going to be bored this year'.
views_timeline.reasoning: Observation of theme transitions in her trend book; yields set by buyer appetite

views_timeline.view: Tariff shock created a new regime: equities fell while yields rose and the dollar fell (vulnerability of US assets, foreign selling, tariff inflation); the episode so far (20-30 days) resembles the start of the tech-bubble drawdown, only the beginning if recession or inflation follows; bonds hard to trade, curve steepener possible; bonds still behaving badly.
views_timeline.reasoning: Overlay of the current drawdown on extended crisis paths; unusual safe-haven behaviour

views_timeline.view: Equities and a weak dollar trended most in 2025; fixed income choppy; energy spiked, reversed and rebounded; metals building long signals on trade tension; current managed-futures drawdown could recover fast or slowly - rebalance into it; further tariff shocks bring smaller reactions and endogenous shocks (monetary policy, inflation) are more likely next and would help trend.
views_timeline.reasoning: The shock has already occurred; fundamentals-based shocks extend

views_timeline.view: US fixed-income trend signals have barely moved despite many themes; the market already prices cuts, so a surprise (more cuts than expected or no cut) is needed; systematic macro did better than trend around Liberation Day (research on economic vs technical trend).
views_timeline.reasoning: SOFR near 3.4% vs fed funds 4.25-4.5%; April 2025 results

views_timeline.view: Trend working again: H1 2025 hard after Liberation Day, H2 better as headlines calm; precious metals surged as hedge with equities and weak dollar; bonds hard because expected US cuts are not delivered; inflation re-emerging in pockets (electricity, healthcare, insurance) matters for next few years; wave of private-wealth money into alternatives coming.
views_timeline.reasoning: Headline noise faded and macro change began to show in prices

views_timeline.view: 2025 saw large return dispersion triggered by Liberation Day: a 10-largest-markets universe beat a broad one because of gold; mid-range speeds (6-8 months) did worst; 2026 will be a boom-and-bust roller coaster with rates lower.
views_timeline.reasoning: Market-set, speed and vol-sizing choices; something brewing in the 2025 macro change

views_timeline.view: January 2026 is a multi-sector trend environment (equities up, weak dollar, precious and base metals up); 2026 looks boom-bust (trend profits on the way up and down) with price trend ahead of macro as fundamentals clear; deglobalisation, policy divergence, geopolitics and trade will keep creating themes over two years; crowding not a major concern.
views_timeline.reasoning: Profits spread across sectors; trend likes disruption; liquid markets, small AUM

views_timeline.view: Q1 2026 was a win for trend: January-February continuing themes, then March pivot to energy and inflation trends offset equity and old-trend losses; faster models handled March better; fixed income remains a headache though FX and energy carry worked; geopolitical risk and oil shocks matter for managed futures.
views_timeline.reasoning: Diversification across asset classes in a pivot; oil shocks weaken the consumer and create inflation shocks

views_timeline.view: Long AI equities, short bonds and long energy/base metals partly hedge each other with an unusual correlation structure that trend likes; fixed income the most difficult sector (higher-for-longer vs oil inflation vs AI growth); no clear equity trend around the conflict; geopolitical tension will be followed by inflation and different asset behaviour over 3-5 years.
views_timeline.reasoning: History rhymes; GPR literature shows inflation after spikes

views_timeline.view: 2026 an ideal year for managed futures; sudden risk-off is the most dangerous scenario for trend now and she senses trends starting to pivot toward a fall narrative (elections, AI concern, risk-off); inflation risk premium from geopolitical risk is being repriced, which should make bond investors nervous; commodities useful again but not to hold passively.
views_timeline.reasoning: Cross-asset themes work at different times; literature shows GPR leads inflation

how_views_changed: The framework (trend follows themes, dispersion is design-driven, inflation breaks bonds, second-responder payoff) is nearly constant across Aug 2024 - Oct 2026; what changes is the year's evidence and emphasis. (1) Speed: Aug 2024 she leans toward shorter signals in a divergent world; 2024 results favour slow/big-market; 2025 punishes the mid-range and favours very slow or very fast; she concludes no speed always wins - reason given: path of the year. (2) Vocabulary: 'crisis alpha' gradually yields to 'second responder' and role-based language (2025-26) because insurance narratives did not help investors hold trend (host's point, which she adopts). (3) Geopolitics moves from a side remark (Jan 2026 preview) to a paper (Jun 2026) to the central thesis for bonds and 60/40 (Oct 2026), citing the GPR-leads-inflation literature. (4) Price vs economic trend: macro ahead in headline-driven 2025, price ahead in early 2026 as fundamentals clarified; she starts macro-vs-technical research in Sep 2025. (5) Bonds: Oct 2024 she notes the classic stock-bond pattern returned at 2-2.5% inflation, but from Apr 2025 'bonds still behaving badly' and by Oct 2026 an inflation premium is being repriced; reasons are the tariff/inflation threat and supply-side geopolitics. (6) Carry: 2024 carry is the threat to crisis alpha; March 2026 FX and energy carry worked (no reconciliation offered). (7) Crowding: 2024 crowded positions rewarded; 2026 not a concern; 2025 she flags capacity-limited markets as untested.

disagreements.topic: Will stock-bond correlation revert to negative? (MT086)
disagreements.their_position: With inflation near 2-2.5% in 2024 the classic risk-off pattern returned; correlation depends on inflation, which comes in waves.
disagreements.other_position: Does not expect a return to the persistent negative correlation of the early decades.

disagreements.topic: Was the 'VIX 65' print a real measure of stress? (MT021)
disagreements.their_position: Might not have been 65 but the number matters anyway as it can feed panic; does not know which came first.
disagreements.other_position: Short window of option quotes while futures were far lower; stress probably overstated.

disagreements.topic: Does divergence help investors? / crisis or correction? (MT021)
disagreements.their_position: More narratives and tactical opportunity after 2020; a reversing correction is not a crisis.
disagreements.other_position: 85-90% of institutional portfolios are convergent, implicitly short vol; a quick crisis can barely hurt trend.

disagreements.topic: How short a trend speed to hold (MT080, MT042)
disagreements.their_position: Diversify speeds; shorter windows give convexity and crisis alpha; best speed changes with the year's path; industry has slowed.
disagreements.other_position: Long lookbacks best in about 70% of the last 25 years (15 of 25 above 200 days); short-term traders index shows almost no performance.

disagreements.topic: Is replication a fair label / why did replicators win 2025? (MT080, MT045)
disagreements.their_position: Use 'beta-like'; judge on tracking error; replicators were smaller in market set and slower, not lucky.
disagreements.other_position: With this tracking error the word is misleading; raises luck or separate alpha.

disagreements.topic: Cause of the 2015-2019 drawdown and value of tariff-based positions (MT045)
disagreements.their_position: Not mainly Trump; very low rates; trends emerge once fundamental data confirm the direction.
disagreements.other_position: Trade-war periods coincide with worst drawdown/recoveries; tariff-based positions are fragile.

disagreements.their_position: Many institutions understand and rebalance after profits.
disagreements.other_position: Rarely sees rebalancing into poor returns; sees selling after good returns.

disagreements.topic: Crowding and capital in trend (MT042, MT220)
disagreements.their_position: AUM small vs liquid markets, crowding overstated; alternative-market lag is a regime effect (gas/power range-bound), crowding untested.
disagreements.other_position: Official AUM understates QIS and in-house trend; inflows to less-liquid markets may have crowded and added cost.

disagreements.their_position: It filters noise and takes the same global trends by another entry method but is an art and can predict trends that never occur.
disagreements.other_position: Pure trend does not anticipate; recent economic-trend success is a 'sunshine' phase that may reverse.

disagreements.topic: Why investors time trend and how to make them hold (MT191)
disagreements.their_position: Any complex liquid strategy suffers; define roles (first/second responder) rather than insurance language.
disagreements.other_position: Daily liquidity and anonymity worsen timing; insurance narratives have not worked.

disagreements.topic: Crisis vs chaos; correlations in sizing; model choice (MT194)
disagreements.their_position: Crisis alpha is a search; different crises need different responders; correlations matter (be sceptical of their vol); dispersion in shocks is positioning luck.
disagreements.other_position: April 2025 is chaos and the classic first responder failed; some CTAs ignore correlation; speed and sizing matter in short periods.

disagreements.topic: March 2026 dispersion and portable alpha separability (MT083)
disagreements.their_position: Energy exposure, speed and design choices explain March; alpha and beta are never fully separated.
disagreements.other_position: Large CTAs are not pure trend (carry/value sleeves); trend on beta consistently outperformed with a cash buffer.

disagreements.topic: Vol sizing and portable alpha packaging (MT195)
disagreements.their_position: Sizing is a spectrum; 'portable alpha' assumes correlations hold; packaging adds classification complexity.
disagreements.other_position: Data show both camps (Sharpe vs return); equity plus trend is portable alpha with trend modulating S&P.

disagreements.their_position: Little disagreement: definition of short-term is broad; reactivity helps fast crises, cost rises with speed; monthly data cannot show slow events.
disagreements.other_position: Short-term trend raises long-run performance if execution is invested in; quarterly/annual horizons might show more.

disagreements.topic: 2024 dispersion size; Liberation Day speeds (MT002, MT134)
disagreements.their_position: 2024 dispersion large due to speed; mid-range 6-8 months overreacted most in 2025, shorter models not as bad.
disagreements.other_position: Beer: not meaningfully larger (2024), slowness helped (2025). Baltas: speed, universe, purity; middle speeds worst locally.

disagreements.topic: High-vol CTA products; dispersion healthy? design obvious? (MT221, MT134)
disagreements.their_position: Daily prints unsmoothed invite performance chasing; dispersion is a challenge and positive; design never obvious, only consistent with an objective.
disagreements.other_position: Carver: half-Kelly 40-50% vol for retail. Brennan: dispersion healthy; Resiminski: unhealthy; Git: diversification.

disagreements.with: Alan Dunn / Rich Brennan / Nick Baltas
disagreements.topic: Is replication an established way to access CTA returns? and the dollar (MT155)
disagreements.their_position: One of many access points, slower but generalised; trend long dollar, short-term continuation, long run unclear.
disagreements.other_position: Dunn: replication established; Brennan: no track record across regimes; Baltas: existential risk; dollar cyclically positive, structurally overvalued.

internal_tensions.issue: Shock effect on trend: 'trend likes chaos, disruption and boom-bust' (we like chaos) vs 'steady markets and sudden shocks are bad for it' and quick reversals give no crisis alpha. Reconciled only informally by shock type (endogenous/extended vs exogenous/reversing), which she stated in July 2025 but not as a rule.

Speed: longer lookbacks have higher Sharpe and she says no speed always wins and speed tilts lack statistical evidence, yet she keeps a speed factor that explains dispersion and argues reactivity is needed for crisis clients; in Aug 2024 she leans shorter, in Oct 2024 praises slow.

Bonds: long/short bond trend 'helped in every equity crisis studied' (and negatively correlated with stocks), yet in April 2025 fixed income offered no offset and bonds are repeatedly 'the hardest sector' (2025-26).

Bond inflation story: 2-2.5% inflation restored the classic risk-off pattern (Oct 2024), yet 'bonds still behaving badly' (Apr 2025) and bonds acceptable whenever yield compensates (Oct 2026); no threshold for inflation or yield given.

Dispersion size: called structurally large and underestimated (MT002), but later she cannot say statistically that 2024 dispersion exceeded history; also 'dispersion is random positioning luck' (coin tosses) vs 'dispersion is a fingerprint of design choices'.

Crowding: crowded positioning was rewarded in 2024 so a crowding measure would have hurt; co-movement says high co-movement signals reversal risk; CTA crowding is overstated; but capacity-limited markets may be a backtest illusion.
Carry: harms crisis alpha in violent events (Aug 2024) vs FX and energy carry worked in March 2026; no conditions given for when carry helps.

Prediction stance: trend 'follows, does not forecast', yet she reads positioning as a recession signal, senses a pivot toward a fall narrative (Oct 2026), and predicts a 2026 boom-bust roller coaster.
Volatility: 'volatility tells the range, not the direction; perfect foresight barely helps' vs speed of vol adjustment decisively changing the return path in 2022 and 2025.

Geopolitical-risk payoff relies on monthly data since 2000 and on large-GPR months (a 'smile'), while crisis alpha is defined as needing sustained weeks-to-months moves; she acknowledges slow events are missed.

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: In high-inflation regimes the stock-bond correlation is positive and bond volatility is about 6% vs about 4% on average; in low-inflation regimes bonds show right-shifted returns in equity-down months.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Long monthly stock/bond returns and CPI back to 1970s (or 800-year series)

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: A long/short bond trend sleeve has negative correlation to equities in equity-down months across inflation regimes, while static bonds do not (positive correlation when inflation is high).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Bond futures or total-return series with 12-month momentum signal; equity returns; inflation regime flag

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Trend (SG Trend or own signals) loses in the first phase of S&P drawdowns below about 15% and earns positive returns only in drawdowns deeper than about 15% or lasting longer (tech bubble, GFC, 2022); short sharp drawdowns (2018, 2020, 2025) give no crisis alpha.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend index or simulated trend returns; S&P drawdown episodes by depth and duration

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Multi-day magnitude-of-surprise shocks (Mahalanobis turbulence) hurt trend and recover within a day or so; correlation surprises mark inflection points with higher manager dispersion; endogenous (policy, inflation) shocks help trend more than exogenous reversing ones.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Daily cross-sectional returns for managers or markets; shock classification

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Trend drawdowns start when equities are making new highs in low-vol periods and recover faster when equities are stressed; the drawdown depth/length can be predicted by equity return regime.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: SG Trend index drawdown episodes vs trailing equity returns and vol

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Rebalancing into trend after drawdowns (and trimming after gains) beats timing: after a very challenging period, one or two strong years typically follow; investor dollar-weighted trend returns lag index returns because of timing.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend index returns, manager flows or fund AUM for dollar-weighted returns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Without the 20 largest months the average trend return falls from about 5.6% to about -0.5%; trend returns are concentrated in a few shock months.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Monthly trend index returns over 30+ years

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Lookback ranking flips year to year: the mid-range (4-9 months) is worst in V-shaped shock years, very short and 12-month windows best in 2025; slow wins in calm trend years (2024); no speed or style factor persists across years.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Single-lookback trend returns by year across markets; persistence tests of style factors

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Months with the largest increases in the geopolitical risk index are followed by 2-3 years of higher inflation; trend earns positive returns in the largest GPR-increase and decrease months, via commodities and bonds not equities.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Caldara-Iacoviello GPR (by country), CPI, trend index, sector returns, monthly since 2000

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Price trend beats economic trend in the worst equity quintiles and in stress; economic trend beats price trend in positive-fundamental years with headline noise (2025); the two are 40-50% correlated.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Price-trend and economic-trend strategy returns split by equity-return quintile

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Excess co-movement (correlation of assets beyond asset-class beta) predicts either reversal or extended trend; used as a filter or risk tool it changes trend risk-adjusted returns.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Cross-asset futures returns; co-movement factor; trend P&L by market

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Slow vol estimators earn more in continuing trends (2022 bond vol doubling, H1 2025) and fast estimators earn more after shocks that reverse (H2 2025); perfect volatility foresight improves trend only marginally.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend simulations with different vol windows and perfect-foresight vol

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Greater carry/non-trend share in CTA portfolios reduces returns in violent short events (Covid, Aug 2024) and lowers crisis-alpha capture.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: CTA style analysis; sleeve returns in crisis months

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Alternative-market trend outperformance in 2020-22 came largely from gas and power and credit (40-50% from gas and power); after those ranged, the outperformance vanished; per-market Sharpe after costs explains the rest.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: 50 traditional vs 120 alternative market trend returns with costs

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Aggregate trend positioning shifting to long bonds and short commodities signals repricing of recession expectations and precedes equity weakness (summer 2024 resembled early 2020).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend positioning (index replication) and subsequent equity returns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Fixed-income trend is strong long in falling rates with a steep curve, strong short with an inverted curve, mixed when flat; bond trend needs a surprise relative to market pricing.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Bond futures trend returns by curve-slope and rate-direction regime; OIS-implied path

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Slow, smaller-market-set replicators beat average CTAs in whipsaw years (2025) and underperform in fast crises; regression-based replication is slowest.
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Replication products vs CTA index by year, lookback/market-set mapping

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Trend allocation of about 15-20% in a 60/40 improves outcomes more when cash rates/inflation are high (Quantica 55/25/20 vs 55/35/10 in low cash rates).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Stock/bond/trend returns by cash-rate regime from 1990

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Stacking trend on equities doubles equity exposure when the trend book is long equities; the combination's joint drawdown depends on trend equity beta (capped or not).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend book equity beta over time; equity+trend drawdowns

testable_hypotheses.hypothesis: Periods of higher geopolitical risk and higher inflation are positive for trend following (her unpublished research preview).
testable_hypotheses.data_needed: Trend returns conditioned on GPR and inflation levels

blind_spots: No explicit stand-alone trading P&L, live track record or risk limits of her own book are given; claims about what 'trend' does rest on indices (SG Trend), papers and client work.
Never gives a threshold for 'high' inflation, for when bonds are cheap enough, or for what crisis depth makes a drawdown 'deep' beyond about 15%.
Rarely addresses transaction costs and capacity quantitatively (except that alternative markets cost more); no numbers on slippage of her own systems.

Valuation, earnings or credit-cycle views are absent; markets are viewed through trend, macro themes and inflation/policy rather than fundamentals; equity-valuation risk (AI) only appears as a theme direction.
Assumes investors can be educated into holding trend; little evidence beyond anecdotes and Quantica 'Paid for Presence'.
Treats the SG Trend Index and style factors as a stable object even though she says indices are not investable and managers drift.
Short samples are often admitted (monthly GPR since 2000, post-1990 Quantica data, one three-day shock) yet implications for the next three to five years are drawn ('history rhymes').
Does not specify how to set the share of risk to equity-long positions in trend when it is stacked with equities beyond 'size dynamically or cap beta'.
Foresight statements (2026 boom-bust, a fall pivot) are given without a stated test.
reader_inferences: (reader) Her operative rule for the 60/40 problem is regime-based: replace some static bond/gold ballast with long/short trend when inflation is above about 2.5%, and add on drawdowns; testable with a CPI regime gate.
(reader) A consistent signal ranking is: Sharpe -> 12-month; convexity/crisis -> add 1-3 month; avoid concentrating in 4-9 month, which she names worst in 2025 and the most common CTA setting.
(reader) She treats the equity-drawdown depth of about 15% as a state variable for whether trend is a first or second responder; this is a natural gating variable for a macro-book overlay.
(reader) Geopolitical-risk index spikes are an observable lead for inflation and commodity/bond-short trends over 2-3 years, giving a macro input independent of price signals.
(reader) Most of her predictions are conditional descriptions of where trend does well, not directional market forecasts, so she is a source of regime-conditional payoff tables rather than views.
(reader) Her emphasis on role, rebalancing and not timing means any strategy built from her ideas should be evaluated as part of a total portfolio and with dollar-weighted (investor) return in mind.
(reader) Her economic-trend vs price-trend point maps to a macro-book design question: macro signals win in headline-noisy but fundamentally clear years; price signals win in stress.
